note: Introductions and plantings from the USGS Nonindigenous Aquatic Species database (records back to the 1870s) plus documented early events. Native fish stocked in their native range, such as most rainbow trout plants, are not in these records; CDFW digital planting records begin in the 2000s.

statewide.text: California creates the Board of Fish Commissioners, the first state fish and game agency in the country, to restock waters depleted by mining and settlement.
American shad are carried west by rail and released into the Sacramento River at Tehama, the first planting of a non-native fish in California by the Fish Commission.
American Shad: first California record, Sacramento River at Tehama.
Common carp are imported from Germany into private ponds in Sonoma Valley; carp spread statewide within two decades.
Common Carp: first California record, state non-specific.
Brook Trout: first California record, North Fork of the American River.
Lake Whitefish: first California record, Clear Lake, 80 NW of Sacramento.
White Catfish: first California record, San Joaquin River near Stockton.
Brown Bullhead: first California record, ponds and sloughs near Sutterville, CA.
Channel Catfish: first California record, San Joaquin River near Stockton.
Atlantic Salmon: first California record, Sacramento River at Redding.
American Eel: first California record, slough of the Sacramento River near Sacramento.
black bass: first California record, Napa Creek, a tributary of San Pablo Bay.
Rock Bass: first California record, Napa Creek, a tributary of San Pablo Bay.
Smallmouth Bass: first California record, Napa River.
Walleye: first California record, Sacramento River opposite Sacramento City.
Tautog: first California record, San Francisco Bay near Oakland.
Black Bullhead: first California record, state non-specific.
Largemouth Bass: first California record, state non-specific.
Yellow Bullhead: first California record, Sacramento River Delta.

Golden trout are carried by hand from Mulkey Creek over the Sierra crest into Cottonwood Creek, the start of moving trout into the fishless high country. Ranchers, miners and later the Sierra Club and the state kept stocking high Sierra lakes, nearly all of which had no fish before.
statewide.source: Inyo National Forest / CDFW golden trout history
